opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most important connection, and the one I'm personally most excited about, is between vision and action, so vision and robotics. For a long time computer vision was treated as a passive problem: you get an image, you label it, you draw boxes around objects. But biologically, vision didn't evolve so animals could write captions. It evolved so they could move around, find food, avoid predators, manipulate things. Perception is for action. So I think the field has to grow up and become embodied: agents that see, move, and learn from the consequences of their movements.

Related to that is the connection to developmental psychology and cognitive science. If you watch a baby, they aren't learning from millions of labeled images. They're poking things, putting things in their mouths, crawling, watching their parents. There's a rich multimodal, interactive stream of experience, and a staged progression: you learn about objects and space and physics before you learn language. I find that a very useful guide. A lot of what we've done in machine learning effectively starts with language, because that's where the data is, and I think we're missing the substrate that sits underneath.

Then of course there's language itself. The large language models have shown what you can do with enormous amounts of text, and connecting vision to language is clearly powerful. But I'd put a caution there. Language is a very compressed, high-level description of the world. A lot of what we know, how to grasp a cup, how to walk on uneven ground, how something will fall, isn't really stored in language. So I see vision and language as complementary, and I'd resist the idea that you can get to general intelligence purely through text.

Neuroscience is another one. Historically there was a lot of cross-fertilization; ideas about receptive fields and hierarchical processing in the visual cortex directly inspired convolutional networks. Now the traffic goes both ways: deep networks are used as models of the ventral stream, and that's productive. I'd like to see more of that, especially around the dorsal stream and visuomotor control, which is less understood.

And finally, applications in science and medicine: microscopy, medical imaging, biology, ecology. Vision is becoming an instrument of science, the way the telescope and microscope were. Automated analysis of huge volumes of visual data will change how discoveries are made.

So if I had to summarize: vision connected to action, connected to how children learn, and connected to the sciences. That's where I think the next couple of decades of interesting work are.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly names vision and robotics and says perception is for action, describing agents that see, move, and learn from their movements.

r002.rationale: It discusses language as a powerful but limited description of the world; it does not present language as a proxy for cognition.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss understanding long-form video or combining language reasoning with visual reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying that computer vision was never really meant to be an isolated field. If you go back to the origins, people like David Marr were explicitly trying to connect what we do computationally with what we understand about biological vision. So I think the connections are part of the DNA of the field, and the question is really which connections are the most fruitful right now.

The first one I would point to is robotics. Vision in nature evolved for action. Animals developed eyes so they could move around, find food, avoid predators. The idea of vision as a passive activity, where you look at a picture and name the objects in it, that is really a construct of the last couple of decades of benchmarks. I think the most exciting work now is bringing perception and control back together. We have had tremendous success in vision because of large datasets, and robotics has been harder precisely because you cannot download a billion examples of a robot manipulating objects. So how do we take the perceptual priors we have learned from images and video and use them to make robots that can learn skills with far less experience? That is a very important open problem, and legged locomotion and dexterous manipulation are where I think we will see real progress.

The second direction is neuroscience and cognitive science, and here I think the flow of ideas should go in both directions. On one hand, deep networks have turned out to be surprisingly good models of certain neural responses in the visual cortex, which is useful for neuroscientists. On the other hand, we should be learning more from how children acquire vision. A child does not get labels. A child gets a continuous stream of video, with the ability to move and interact, and over the first year or two they develop a pretty sophisticated understanding of objects and space and other agents. Developmental psychology gives us a kind of curriculum, and I think we should take it seriously as a guide for how to build systems that learn from much less supervision.

The third is language. There has been an enormous amount of progress in natural language processing, and the connection to vision is obvious because so much of what we want to communicate about is grounded in the visual world. But I would caution against thinking that language is the solution to vision. A lot of visual understanding is not verbalizable. Think about what a surgeon or a carpenter knows about the geometry and physics of what they are handling. Very little of that is in words. So I see vision and language as complementary, and the interesting questions are about where the grounding actually comes from.

And finally, I would mention the broader connections to science and medicine. Vision techniques are now routinely used in biology, in astronomy, in medical imaging, in understanding climate data. These applications are important in themselves, but they also push us. They give us problems where the data looks nothing like natural images, where there are no human labels to speak of, and where getting things right matters a great deal. I think that discipline is good for the field.

So if I had to summarize, I would say the direction I care about most is moving from vision as recognition to vision as understanding, and understanding ultimately means being able to act in the world, to predict what will happen next, and to connect what you see with what you know. That requires us to talk to the roboticists, the neuroscientists, the linguists, and the domain scientists, and I think that is where the next decade is going to be.

r001.rationale: It connects vision to robotics by saying vision evolved for action and emphasizes bringing perception and control together.

r002.rationale: It describes vision and language as complementary, but does not present language as a proxy for cognition.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss long-form video or combining language reasoning with visual reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most important connections is between vision and robotics. We often study vision as if the goal were simply to describe an image: these are the objects, these are their locations. But for an agent acting in the world, perception has to support action. Can I pick this object up? What will happen if I push it? And action, in turn, gives you new information about what you are seeing.

That connects vision to learning and to our understanding of intelligence. A child doesn’t learn about the world just by looking at labeled pictures. The child moves around, touches things, and observes consequences. How do we build systems that can learn through that kind of interaction?

There’s also a very interesting connection to language. Language lets us communicate about the world, but the concepts have to connect to perception and experience. So, to me, a central open direction is understanding how perception, action, and language can develop together.

r001.rationale: It says vision for robotics must support action and explains how acting can provide new information about what is seen.

r002.rationale: It connects language with perception and experience, but does not present language as a proxy for cognition.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss long-form video or combining language and visual reasoning to understand it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one very important direction is the connection between vision and robotics. We often study vision as if its purpose were simply to produce a description of an image. But for an agent acting in the world, perception has to support action: Where can I move? What can I grasp? What will happen if I push this object? And action, in turn, gives you new visual information. So perception and action really belong together.

Another direction is the connection to language. Language lets us communicate about what we see, but it also raises the question of grounding: How do words and concepts acquire meaning through experience of the world? Recognizing an object in a photograph is only one part of understanding it.

And then there are the connections to neuroscience and developmental psychology. A child learns through looking, moving, touching, and interacting with people. Understanding how those sources of information come together could help us build systems that learn more effectively. To me, the interesting challenge is to connect these capabilities into an agent that can perceive, learn, and act.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly connects vision and robotics through perception that supports action, including movement and grasping.

r002.rationale: It discusses language and grounding concepts in worldly experience, but does not present language as a proxy for cognition.

r003.rationale: It does not mention long-form video or combining language reasoning with visual reasoning.
